text: Welcome to Build a Real-Time System. Over this course we are going to build, from raw TCP up, a live collaboration app that I'm going to call Pulse. Pulse is a chat room with a presence board on the side, so you see messages arrive the instant someone types them, and you see who is online, who just left, and who has gone quiet. Before we write a single line, I want to answer a question that sounds obvious and really isn't. What actually makes a system real-time? Because if you ask ten engineers, you will get ten answers, and most of them will be about speed.

Here is my definition. A real-time system is one where the server can tell the client something the moment it happens, without the client having to ask. Notice what that says. It isn't about milliseconds. A system that updates in two hundred milliseconds but only when you refresh the page is not real-time in this sense. A system that pushes a message within one second, unprompted, is. The key idea is the direction of initiation. In plain HTTP the client always speaks first. In a real-time system, the server gets to speak first too.

Now there's a second meaning of real-time that you may have heard, the hard real-time of flight controllers and pacemakers, where missing a deadline is a failure. That is not what we are building, okay? Pulse is what people call soft real-time, or near real-time. If a chat message arrives in eighty milliseconds instead of forty, nobody is hurt. What matters is that delivery is push-based, low latency on average, and that we handle the ugly cases, like a client vanishing without saying goodbye, which we will spend a whole chapter on.

So what makes this hard? Three things, and they map directly onto the chapters ahead. First, state. A normal HTTP server forgets you after each response, but a real-time server has to remember every connected client, which room they're in, and whether they're still alive. Second, fan-out. One message in becomes a thousand messages out, and doing that efficiently is its own problem. Third, scale. The moment you run two server processes, client A on server one cannot see client B on server two, unless you build something to connect them.

Let me give you the roadmap, so you know where we're headed. Chapter two goes below the WebSocket API and builds the handshake and the frame parser ourselves, using only Node's net and crypto modules. Chapter three accepts connections, keeps a client registry and broadcasts. Chapter four adds rooms and pub/sub. Chapter five adds heartbeats and presence. Chapter six brings in Redis pub/sub and Redis Streams. Chapter seven scales Pulse horizontally behind a load balancer. Each lecture ends with working code, and you should be typing along with me.

One more thing about how I teach this. We will not use the popular ws or socket.io libraries for the core of the course. That's deliberate. When you've written the code that computes the Sec-WebSocket-Accept header and the code that unmasks a frame payload, the libraries stop being magic. You'll be able to read their source, debug them at three in the morning, and know what a proxy is doing to your connection. In the next lecture we compare polling, long-polling and WebSockets, so that the reason we picked WebSockets is earned, not assumed.

In this lecture we answer a practical question. If the server needs to push data to a browser, what are the options, and why did the industry end up at WebSockets? We'll look at three approaches, polling, long-polling and WebSockets, and for each one I want us to think about three costs: latency, wasted work, and how much connection state the server has to carry. I'll sketch tiny versions of each so the trade-offs are concrete, and then we'll know what Pulse actually needs.

Start with plain polling. The client runs a setInterval, say every two seconds, and calls `fetch('/messages?since=' plus the last id)`. The server answers with whatever is new, usually nothing. This is wonderfully simple and works through every proxy on earth. But look at the costs. Average latency is half the interval, so one second here. And if ten thousand users are watching a quiet room, you are serving five thousand requests a second to say nothing, each one carrying full HTTP headers and possibly a fresh authentication check.

You might think, fine, just poll faster. Poll every two hundred milliseconds. Now latency is better, but you have multiplied the wasted work by ten. That's the fundamental trap of polling, latency and load trade against each other directly. You can only buy freshness by burning requests. For a dashboard that refreshes once a minute, that's a perfectly good deal, and I would use polling happily. For a chat room where people expect a reply to show up instantly, it is the wrong tool.

Long-polling is the clever fix. The client sends a request, but the server deliberately doesn't answer until it has something to say, or until a timeout of say thirty seconds. When data arrives, the server responds, and the client immediately opens the next request. Latency is now excellent, because the response is already waiting. And the wasted requests mostly vanish. This is what Comet and early Facebook chat did. The cost is that every waiting client holds an open request, and after each message there's a reconnect gap in which events can slip by unless you track ids carefully.

There's also a hidden cost in long-polling: each message still pays for a whole HTTP round trip with headers, and the client cannot send while it waits, it needs a second request for that. So you are using two channels badly. WebSockets fix this by upgrading a single HTTP connection into a persistent, full-duplex, message-oriented pipe. After a one-time handshake, either side can send a small frame at any moment. The overhead per message drops to two to fourteen bytes of framing, instead of hundreds of bytes of headers.

So the trade is this. WebSockets give us the lowest latency and the lowest per-message overhead, but they cost us statefulness. Every client is a long-lived socket that lives in one specific process's memory, and that decision will haunt us in chapters six and seven when we scale. Polling is stateless and easy to scale but slow or wasteful. For Pulse, a chat plus presence board, we want instant push in both directions, so WebSockets it is. Next lecture, let's pin down exactly what we are building.

Time to define the thing we are building. Pulse is a collaborative chat room with a live presence board. You open it in a browser, pick a name, join a room like general or design, and you see two things. A scrolling list of messages, and a sidebar of everyone currently in the room with a green dot for active and a grey dot for idle. When a person joins, leaves, or their laptop lid closes, the sidebar updates for everyone within a few seconds.

Let me show you the file layout so we all type the same names. Inside a project folder called pulse, there is a `src` directory. `src/server.js` is the entry point and owns the TCP server. `src/handshake.js` computes the upgrade response. `src/frame.js` encodes and decodes WebSocket frames. `src/registry.js` keeps track of connected clients. `src/rooms.js` holds the pub/sub rooms. `src/heartbeat.js` runs ping and pong, and `src/presence.js` derives who is online. Later we add `src/bus.js` for Redis and `src/stream.js` for history.

Two constraints I'm setting now, so there are no surprises. First, the server is plain Node, version twenty or newer, with zero dependencies for the WebSocket layer. We'll use `net` for TCP and `crypto` for SHA-1 and base64. Redis will arrive in chapter six, and we'll use the `redis` client package for that, since writing the Redis protocol is not today's problem. Second, the browser side is deliberately small, one `public/index.html` that uses the native `WebSocket` API. All the interesting engineering is on the server.

Here's the message format, because it shapes everything. Every message that Pulse sends is a JSON text frame with a `type` field. A client sends `{ type: 'join', room: 'general', name: 'asha' }` to enter a room, and `{ type: 'say', room: 'general', text: 'hello' }` to chat. The server replies with `{ type: 'message', room, from, text, ts }` and `{ type: 'presence', room, users: [...] }`. Keeping the protocol this boring is on purpose. It lets us focus on transport and scale, not on schema design.

Let me also tell you what Pulse will survive by the end. It will survive a client closing the tab, a client losing wifi without any close frame, a server restart that drops all sockets, and, by chapter seven, three server processes behind a load balancer where users on different processes still see each other's messages. Each of those is a real failure mode that toy tutorials skip. I want you to leave with a system you could actually defend in a design review.

So, the plan for the next stretch. Chapter two is the part most people never see. We'll open a raw TCP socket, read an HTTP upgrade request by hand, compute the accept key, and then parse binary frames byte by byte. It's the hardest chapter conceptually, but also the one that pays off the most. Create your pulse folder, run `npm init -y`, make the `src` directory, and I'll meet you in the next lecture, where we start with TCP itself.

Before we touch WebSockets, I want to spend one lecture on what's underneath, because every confusing WebSocket bug eventually turns out to be a TCP fact in disguise. TCP gives you a reliable, ordered, bidirectional stream of bytes between two endpoints. Reliable means lost packets are retransmitted. Ordered means bytes come out in the order they went in. And stream is the word to underline. TCP has no idea where one message ends and the next begins. It just gives you bytes.

Let me prove that with code. Open a new file, `src/tcp-demo.js`, and write `const net = require('node:net')`. Then `net.createServer((socket) => { socket.on('data', (chunk) => console.log(chunk.length, chunk.toString())) }).listen(4000)`. Now in another terminal run `nc localhost 4000` and type hello, press enter, type world, press enter. You'll typically see two data events. But if you pipe in a large file, you will see chunks of arbitrary size, none of which line up with what you wrote. That is the stream nature of TCP.

This matters enormously for us. When a browser sends a WebSocket frame, the bytes of that frame can arrive split across two data events, or two frames can arrive glued together in one event. If our parser assumes one data event equals one message, it will work on your laptop and break in production under load. So a rule I'll repeat in chapter two: we always buffer incoming bytes, and we only consume a frame when we have all of it.

Second TCP fact. A connection is identified by four things, source address, source port, destination address and destination port. The server listens on one port, but every client gets its own socket on it. In Node, each connection event hands you a `net.Socket`, which is a duplex stream, so you can read from it and write to it. Remember this, because our client registry in chapter three is literally a collection of these socket objects. Third fact, and this one bites everyone. TCP only tells you a peer is gone in two ways. A clean close, where the peer sends a FIN and you get an `end` event, or a reset, where you get an `error` event. If a laptop loses wifi or a phone goes into a tunnel, neither happens. Your side just sits there thinking the connection is fine, sometimes for minutes. This is called a half-open connection. It is the entire reason ping and pong exist in the WebSocket protocol, and we'll build that in chapter five.

Fourth, a quick note on Nagle's algorithm and latency. By default TCP may delay small writes to batch them into bigger packets. For a chat app that's a bad trade, because we want each small message out immediately. In Node you call `socket.setNoDelay(true)`, and we will do that for every Pulse client. Write that on a sticky note. Small thing, noticeable difference in feel. Let's close the loop. HTTP is just a text protocol that runs on top of this byte stream. A request is a line like `GET /chat HTTP/1.1`, then header lines, then a blank line made of carriage return and line feed. WebSocket begins life as exactly such a request, and then, once both sides agree, the same TCP connection stops speaking HTTP and starts speaking binary frames. That agreement is the upgrade handshake, and it's the subject of the next lecture.

A WebSocket connection starts as an ordinary HTTP request. That's by design, so it can pass through firewalls and share port eighty or four forty-three with normal web traffic. Open `src/handshake.js` with me. We are going to read the upgrade request off the raw socket, validate it, and build the response. First, let me show you what the browser actually sends, because you should see it with your own eyes. Run a tiny `net` server that logs the first chunk, and point `new WebSocket('ws://localhost:4000/chat')` at it from the browser console.

You will see something like this. A first line, `GET /chat HTTP/1.1`. Then `Host: localhost:4000`, `Upgrade: websocket`, `Connection: Upgrade`, `Sec-WebSocket-Key: ` followed by a base64 string, and `Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13`. Possibly an `Origin` header and `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions` too. Each line ends with carriage return, line feed, and the headers end with a blank line, so the byte sequence is backslash r backslash n twice. That double CRLF is how we know the request is complete. Now why does the server have to answer in a special way? The point of the key is not security of the data. It's a proof that the server understood the WebSocket protocol, so that a confused HTTP server or a cache can't accidentally be tricked into treating the connection as a WebSocket. RFC 6455 says the server takes the client's `Sec-WebSocket-Key`, appends a fixed magic string, the GUID `258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11`, hashes the result with SHA-1, and base64 encodes the digest. That value goes into `Sec-WebSocket-Accept`.

Let's write it. In `handshake.js`: `const crypto = require('node:crypto')`, and `const GUID = '258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11'`. Then `function acceptKey(key) { return crypto.createHash('sha1').update(key + GUID).digest('base64') }`. That's the entire cryptographic part. You can test it with the example straight from the RFC: the key `dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==` must produce `s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=`. Put that in a test now, because if this is off by a character, the browser will silently refuse the connection. Next, parsing. We buffer data until we see the double CRLF with `buffer.indexOf('\r\n\r\n')`. Then we split the header block on CRLF, take the first line as the request line, and build a lowercase header map by splitting each line at the first colon. We validate: the method must be GET, `upgrade` must equal websocket ignoring case, `connection` must contain the token upgrade, the version must be 13, and a key must exist. If anything fails, we write `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` and destroy the socket. Never trust the first bytes from the network.

The success response is exactly this, written as text. `HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols`, then `Upgrade: websocket`, then `Connection: Upgrade`, then `Sec-WebSocket-Accept:` and our computed value, then a blank line. We call `socket.write` with those lines joined by CRLF. Status 101 is the key moment. From the byte after that blank line, nothing on this socket is HTTP anymore. Also remember the leftover bytes: if the client already sent a frame in the same chunk after the headers, we must slice them off and hand them to the frame parser instead of dropping them.

A couple of production notes. Check the `Origin` header against an allow-list, since browsers don't apply the same-origin policy to WebSockets, and otherwise any web page could open a socket to your server using the visitor's cookies. That's called cross-site WebSocket hijacking. And if you support subprotocols, you'd echo back one chosen value in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. For Pulse we skip subprotocols. Now we have an open pipe. Next lecture, what travels down it: the frame format.

Now the lecture I promised was the hardest, and I want to make it feel easy. After the 101 response, both sides exchange frames. A frame is a small binary envelope around a payload. We're going to read the layout from RFC 6455, then write `src/frame.js` with a `decodeFrame` function and an `encodeFrame` function. I'll go bit by bit, and I'd suggest keeping a pen and paper handy, because drawing the bytes makes this click. The first byte holds two things. The top bit is FIN, which says this is the final fragment of a message. The next three bits are reserved, RSV1 to RSV3, which must be zero unless you negotiated an extension like permessage-deflate. The low four bits are the opcode. Opcode 0x1 means text, 0x2 means binary, 0x0 means a continuation of a fragmented message, 0x8 is close, 0x9 is ping, and 0xA is pong. In code, `const fin = (b0 & 0x80) !== 0` and `const opcode = b0 & 0x0f`.

The second byte holds the MASK bit on top and a seven-bit payload length below it. `const masked = (b1 & 0x80) !== 0` and `let len = b1 & 0x7f`. If len is up to 125, that's the actual length. If it's 126, the real length is in the next two bytes as a big-endian unsigned sixteen-bit integer, so we use `buf.readUInt16BE(2)`. If it's 127, the next eight bytes hold a sixty-four-bit length, and in Node we'd use `readBigUInt64BE(2)`, and I recommend rejecting anything absurdly large, say over a megabyte, so a hostile client can't make us allocate gigabytes.

Next comes the masking key, four random bytes, present only if the mask bit is set. And here's a rule you must remember: every frame sent from client to server must be masked, and every frame sent from server to client must not be. Why? It isn't encryption. It's to stop a malicious page from crafting bytes that a transparent proxy might mistake for an HTTP response, a cache-poisoning attack. As a server, if we receive an unmasked client frame, the RFC says we should close the connection with a protocol error.

Unmasking is a simple loop. For each byte i of the payload, `payload[i] = payload[i] ^ maskKey[i % 4]`. XOR with the repeating four-byte key. Because XOR is its own inverse, the same operation masks and unmasks. So `decodeFrame(buf)` reads the header, checks that `buf.length` is at least header length plus payload length, and if not, returns null, meaning wait for more bytes. If the frame is complete, it returns the opcode, fin flag, unmasked payload, and the total number of bytes consumed, so the caller can slice them off the buffer.

Now encoding, the easier direction, since server frames aren't masked. For a text message, we convert the string with `Buffer.from(text)`. Then if the length is under 126 the header is two bytes: `0x81` for FIN plus text opcode, and the length. If it's under 65536 the header is four bytes: `0x81`, 126, then the length as two bytes. Otherwise ten bytes, with 127 and an eight-byte length. We concatenate header and payload with `Buffer.concat`. The same function takes an opcode, so ping is `encodeFrame(0x9, empty)`.

Two more details to handle correctly. Close frames, opcode 0x8, carry an optional two-byte status code, like 1000 for normal closure, 1001 for going away, and 1002 for a protocol error, followed by a reason string. And fragmentation: a big message may arrive as a text frame with FIN zero, followed by continuation frames with opcode zero, ending with FIN one. We'll buffer fragments until FIN. Write a unit test now: encode a message, mask it manually, decode it, and compare. In chapter three we plug this into a live server.

Time to put the handshake and the frame code together into a running server. Open `src/server.js`. At the top, `const net = require('node:net')`, then we import `acceptKey` and `parseUpgrade` from `./handshake` and `encodeFrame` and `decodeFrame` from `./frame`. We create the TCP server with `net.createServer(onConnection)` and listen on port 4000. The interesting question is how a single socket moves through two phases, handshake and then frames, so let's model that explicitly. Inside `onConnection(socket)` we create a small state object: `const conn = { socket, state: 'handshake', buffer: Buffer.alloc(0), id: nextId++ }`. Then `socket.setNoDelay(true)` for latency, and `socket.on('data', (chunk) => { conn.buffer = Buffer.concat([conn.buffer, chunk]); drain(conn) })`. Every chunk is appended and then we try to make progress. A function called drain is the heart of it, and it switches on `conn.state`.

In the handshake state, drain looks for the double CRLF in the buffer. If it's not there yet, it returns and waits for the next chunk. If it is, it parses the request, writes the 101 response using our `acceptKey`, slices the header bytes off the buffer, sets `conn.state = 'open'`, and then falls through to keep draining, because frame bytes may already be sitting behind the headers. That fall-through is the bug people forget, and it shows up as a client whose first message mysteriously vanishes.

In the open state, drain loops. `while (true) { const frame = decodeFrame(conn.buffer); if (!frame) break; conn.buffer = conn.buffer.subarray(frame.consumed); handleFrame(conn, frame) }`. Each iteration consumes exactly one complete frame. When decodeFrame returns null we simply wait. This loop is what makes us robust against both split frames and glued frames, which we talked about in the TCP lecture. It's short, but it's the most important loop in the project. Now handleFrame, a switch on opcode. For 0x1 text we decode the payload as UTF-8 and call `onMessage(conn, text)`, which for now just logs it and echoes it back with `conn.socket.write(encodeFrame(0x1, Buffer.from(text)))`. For 0x8 close we reply with a close frame echoing the status code, then call `socket.end()`. For 0x9 ping we answer with a pong, opcode 0xA, carrying the same payload, which the RFC requires. For 0xA pong we'll ignore it until chapter five. Anything unknown, we close with 1002.

Let's test it. Start the server with `node src/server.js`. In the browser console, `const ws = new WebSocket('ws://localhost:4000'); ws.onmessage = (e) => console.log(e.data); ws.onopen = () => ws.send('hello pulse')`. You should see hello pulse come straight back. Congratulations, that's a real WebSocket server with no libraries. Open the network tab and look at the frames panel to see your text frame and the echo, and notice the browser reports them as masked going out and unmasked coming back.

Before moving on, one consideration about timeouts. A client that opens a TCP connection and never completes the handshake costs us a socket forever, which is a classic slowloris-style attack. So when a connection arrives, start a timer, say five seconds, and if the state is still handshake when it fires, destroy the socket. Cancel the timer once the upgrade succeeds. Also cap the handshake buffer at around eight kilobytes, because someone could stream endless header bytes at us without ever sending the blank line. Small guards, but they are the difference between a demo and a server.

Last piece for this lecture, error and close handling on the socket. `socket.on('error', () => socket.destroy())`, because an unhandled error event on a socket will crash the whole Node process, and one flaky client must never be able to take Pulse down. And `socket.on('close', () => cleanup(conn))`. Cleanup does nothing yet, but in the next lecture it will remove the connection from a registry, and that registry is the next thing we build.

Right now our server echoes to whoever sent the message, and it forgets everyone else exists. To do anything interesting, like chat, we need to know who is connected. That's the client registry, and we'll write it in `src/registry.js`. The core of it is just a Map from connection id to a client record. But the design choices around that map decide how easy rooms, presence and scaling will be later, so let's think before typing. What should a client record contain? At minimum, the id, the socket, a display name once they've introduced themselves, the set of rooms they've joined, a timestamp for last activity, and a flag called isAlive that we'll use for heartbeats. So, `{ id, socket, name: null, rooms: new Set(), lastSeen: Date.now(), isAlive: true }`. Notice I'm keeping the record plain data plus the socket. No methods, no class hierarchy. Plain objects are easy to log, and later easy to describe over Redis.

Now the registry API, kept tiny. `const clients = new Map()`. `function add(conn)` creates the record and stores it with `clients.set(conn.id, record)`. `function remove(id)` deletes it and returns the record, so callers can clean up rooms. `function get(id)`, and `function all()` returning `clients.values()`. Export those. Why a Map and not a plain object or an array? Map gives us constant-time insert, lookup and delete by key, and insertion-order iteration, which makes our logs predictable. Wire it in. In `server.js`, in `onConnection`, after the handshake succeeds we call `registry.add(conn)`. In the `close` handler we call `registry.remove(conn.id)`. And in the handler for a message of type `hello` we set `record.name`. Add a log line, `console.log('clients:', registry.size())`, and open three browser tabs. Close one, and you should see the count go down. If it doesn't drop, your close handler isn't running, and that's a leak we're about to talk about.

Leaks are the number one operational problem of a real-time server. Every long-lived connection holds a socket, buffers, and your own bookkeeping. If you add to a Map on connect and forget to remove on every exit path, the process slowly fills with ghosts. There are several exit paths: clean close frame, socket end, socket error, a protocol violation where we destroy it ourselves, and a heartbeat timeout later. So I like to funnel all of them through one function, `dropClient(id, reason)`, which is idempotent, safe to call twice.

A subtle point on identity. Should the registry key be the socket, a generated id, or the user name? Not the name, because one person can open two tabs, and names can collide. Not the raw socket as a public identifier, because we'll want to put ids in messages and logs. A monotonically increasing integer works for one process, but in chapter seven, with several processes, ids must be globally unique, so use `crypto.randomUUID()` right now and save yourself a migration.

Let's also add a safety valve. A `MAX_CLIENTS` constant, say ten thousand, and in the upgrade path, if `registry.size() >= MAX_CLIENTS`, answer with `HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable` and close. Real servers are bounded by file descriptors and memory, and it's better to refuse politely than to fall over. Now we have an authoritative list of live connections, and the next lecture uses it for the headline feature: broadcasting a message to everybody.

Broadcasting is the first moment Pulse feels like a product. One person sends a line of text, and every connected tab shows it. With the registry, the implementation is almost embarrassingly short, but there are four or five traps in it, and I want us to walk into each one deliberately. Open `src/server.js` and add a function `broadcast(payload, exceptId)`. The naive version: `for (const client of registry.all()) { client.socket.write(frame) }`. And the first optimization is already visible. We should encode the frame once, outside the loop, `const frame = encodeFrame(0x1, Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(payload)))`, and write the same Buffer to every socket. Encoding per recipient would mean a thousand clients cause a thousand JSON stringifications and a thousand allocations, for exactly the same bytes. Server frames are unmasked, so the bytes really are identical for everyone.

Trap number two, the sender. Sometimes you want the sender to receive their own message, which makes the UI simpler because there's one code path for rendering, and sometimes you don't. That's the `exceptId` parameter. For Pulse chat we'll echo to everyone including the sender, because the server adds the timestamp and a message id, and we want every client to show the canonical version. For presence updates we'll sometimes skip the subject. Having the option costs nothing.

Trap number three, writing to a dead or slow socket. `socket.write` returns false when the internal buffer is above the high water mark, which means the peer is not keeping up. If we ignore that, a single slow client causes the Node process to buffer unbounded data in memory, and a thousand slow clients will kill the server. So in broadcast we check `socket.writableLength`. If it exceeds, say, one megabyte, we drop that client with close code 1008, policy violation, rather than let it hurt everyone. This is called backpressure handling, and most tutorials skip it.

Trap number four, mutation during iteration. If writing to a socket throws synchronously, or we decide to drop a client in the middle of the loop, we're deleting from the Map while iterating it. Map iteration in JavaScript is actually safe against deletion, but the cleaner habit is to collect the offenders in an array and drop them after the loop. Also wrap each write in try and catch. One broken socket must never prevent the other nine hundred and ninety-nine from getting the message.

Now wire the message handler. When a text frame arrives, we `JSON.parse` it inside a try and catch, because clients can send garbage. If `msg.type === 'say'`, we build `{ type: 'message', from: record.name, text: msg.text, ts: Date.now() }`, and call `broadcast`. Also validate: name must be set, text must be a string, and cap its length at, say, two thousand characters. Open four tabs, and chat between them. That's the first end-to-end Pulse. Before we move on, think about what this design cannot do. Every message goes to every client. In a real app, you'd have many conversations, and nobody wants messages from a room they never joined. That's the problem rooms solve, and the cost of this broadcast loop, linear in the number of clients, is something we'll have to look at carefully. In chapter four we'll introduce rooms and channels, and turn our single broadcast into targeted fan-out.

We have one global broadcast, and now we want to split the world into conversations. Pulse will have rooms named general, design, random and so on. A client joins a room, receives only that room's traffic, and can be in several rooms at once. In the pub/sub vocabulary, a room is a channel, and the pattern is publish-subscribe: publishers send to a channel without knowing who listens, and subscribers listen without knowing who publishes. Let's build it in `src/rooms.js`.

The data structure first. We need to answer two questions fast. Given a room, who's in it? And given a client, which rooms are they in, so we can clean up on disconnect? So we keep two indexes. `const rooms = new Map()` maps a room name to a Set of client ids. And each client record already has `rooms`, a Set of room names. Two indexes, kept in sync by the only two functions that mutate them. It's a little redundant, but it turns disconnect cleanup from a scan of every room into a loop over a handful.

Why store ids in the Set and not the socket objects themselves? Two reasons. One, ids are serializable, and when we move to Redis, a room's membership might be described across processes. Two, there is a single source of truth for the socket, the registry, so a socket can never be kept alive by a stale reference in some room. The rooms module asks the registry for the socket at send time, and if the client has gone, it simply skips and prunes.

Think about naming too. A room name is user input, so we validate it: lowercase letters, digits and dashes, maximum thirty-two characters, using a regular expression like `/^[a-z0-9-]{1,32}$/`. Otherwise someone can create a room called with a million characters, or one that collides with an internal channel name. Also decide on a cap on rooms per client, say twenty, because an unbounded Set per client is a memory attack waiting to happen. Rooms get created lazily. The first join creates the Set, and when the last member leaves, we delete the Map entry. That second part matters. Without it, a long-running server accumulates thousands of empty room entries from rooms that existed for ten seconds. In code: after removing a member, `if (set.size === 0) rooms.delete(name)`. Empty-room garbage collection is one of those unglamorous lines that separates a demo from a service.

Let me show a concrete picture, so the structure is not abstract. Suppose Asha and Ben are in general, Ben and Chen are in design. The rooms Map holds general mapping to a Set of two ids, and design mapping to a Set of two ids. Ben's own record lists both room names. When Ben's socket closes, we read his record, see general and design, remove his id from each Set, and we are done in two operations. Without the second index, we would have scanned every room in the server, which at ten thousand rooms is exactly the sort of hidden cost that makes disconnect storms painful. So here's the shape of `rooms.js`. It exports `join(clientId, room)`, `leave(clientId, room)`, `leaveAll(clientId)`, `members(room)`, and `publish(room, payload)`. The next lecture implements join and leave, with the edge cases, and the one after that implements publish, the fan-out. Keep the `rooms` Map and the validation function open in your editor, and let's move on to subscribing.

Let me show a concrete picture, so the structure is not abstract. Suppose Asha and Ben are in general, Ben and Chen are in design. The rooms Map holds general mapping to a Set of two ids, and design mapping to a Set of two ids. Ben's own record lists both room names. When Ben's socket closes, we read his record, see general and design, remove his id from each Set, and we are done in two operations. Without the second index, we would have scanned every room in the server, which at ten thousand rooms is exactly the sort of hidden cost that makes disconnect storms painful.

Let's implement subscribe and unsubscribe. In `src/rooms.js`, `join(clientId, room)` does the following. Validate the name. Look up the client in the registry and return an error if it's missing. Check the per-client cap. Then `let set = rooms.get(room); if (!set) { set = new Set(); rooms.set(room, set) }`, `set.add(clientId)`, and `client.rooms.add(room)`. Return true if the membership was actually new, because Sets make double-joins harmless, and we want to know whether to announce anything. That boolean matters. If a client sends join for general twice, because of a buggy retry or a reconnect race, the second call should be a no-op, and shouldn't produce a second join announcement. So the contract is idempotent: calling join twice leaves the same state as calling it once. Idempotency is a theme in distributed systems, and it will save you repeatedly when messages are retried. Same for leave: leaving a room you're not in does nothing and doesn't throw.

Now `leave(clientId, room)`. Get the Set, delete the id, delete the room name from the client's own Set, and if the room Set is now empty, delete the room from the Map. And `leaveAll(clientId)` just iterates a copy of the client's rooms and calls leave for each. Why a copy? Because leave mutates the client's Set while we iterate, and while JavaScript tolerates it, copying with `[...client.rooms]` makes the intent obvious and avoids surprises. Hook these to the protocol. In the message handler, `type: 'join'` calls `rooms.join(record.id, msg.room)`, and `type: 'leave'` calls leave. When a client joins, we send them an acknowledgement, `{ type: 'joined', room }`, so the UI can switch views. And crucially, we update the disconnect path: in `dropClient` we call `rooms.leaveAll(id)` before `registry.remove(id)`. If you forget this, the Set holds ids of clients that no longer exist, and every publish has to step over them forever.

A common bug here is the ordering race on disconnect. Imagine the socket closes at the same moment we're in the middle of a publish loop. The publish loop reads a member id, asks the registry for the record, and it's gone. So publish must tolerate missing records, which is why I said earlier that rooms store ids instead of sockets. If the lookup fails, skip it, and queue that id for pruning. Never assume that membership and liveness are perfectly in sync.

Also think about authorization even though Pulse is simple. Is every client allowed to join any room? In a real product, private rooms need a check at join time, and not at message time. That check belongs in `join`, returning a reason string, so the handler can answer `{ type: 'error', code: 'forbidden' }`. Put a hook in now: a function `canJoin(client, room)` that always returns true, and replace it when you add real auth. Let me add one more practical consideration, which is what the client sees. A join request can fail for several reasons: invalid room name, too many rooms, forbidden, or the client hasn't introduced itself yet. Don't just close the socket on these. Send a structured error back, `{ type: 'error', code: 'bad_room', ref: 'join' }`, so the UI can show a message and stay connected. Reserve closing the connection for protocol violations, like malformed frames or oversized payloads, where continuing is unsafe. That distinction between application errors and protocol errors keeps your server friendly to well-behaved clients and strict with abusive ones.

Let's test it. Open three tabs, join two of them to general and one to design, and log `rooms.members('general')`. You should see two ids. Close a tab and check that the room shrinks, and that closing the last member removes the room entirely. Our registry and membership are consistent, so next we make rooms useful: a publish that sends a message only to the members of one room. That's fan-out.

Fan-out is the act of taking one incoming message and delivering it to many recipients. It's the operation a real-time system spends most of its time on, so it deserves care. In `rooms.js`, we write `publish(room, payload, exceptId)`. It's our broadcast function from chapter three, but scoped. First line: `const set = rooms.get(room); if (!set) return 0`. Return the number of recipients, because that's useful for metrics and tests. Then the same optimizations as before. Encode once: `const frame = encodeFrame(0x1, Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(payload)))`. Loop over the ids in the Set. For each, `const client = registry.get(id)`; if it's missing, add the id to a `stale` array and continue. Otherwise check backpressure with `client.socket.writableLength`, and write the frame inside a try and catch. After the loop, remove the stale ids from the room. That gives us correctness and a self-healing membership list.

Let's talk about cost. Publishing to a room of N members is O(N) writes, and that's unavoidable, since N sockets need N writes. What we can control is the constant factor, which is why we encode once, and why we don't do any per-recipient allocation. At ten thousand members and ten messages per second, that's a hundred thousand socket writes per second. Node can do that on one core, but only because each write is small and the work per recipient is tiny. Anything heavier per recipient, like per-user filtering, changes the math quickly.

Which brings up per-recipient customization. Suppose a message should render differently for the sender, for instance with an isMine flag. Don't compute it on the server per recipient. Send the same bytes to everyone and let the client compare `msg.from` with its own name. Fan-out is fastest when the payload is identical for all recipients, and that is a design principle worth carrying into any real-time system you build. Now update the chat handler: when a `say` message arrives, check that the sender is actually a member of that room, `record.rooms.has(msg.room)`, and reject otherwise. Then `rooms.publish(msg.room, { type: 'message', room: msg.room, from: record.name, text, ts: Date.now() })`. Without that membership check, any client could post into any room they hadn't joined, bypassing whatever access control we add at join time. Authorization at the choke point, always.

Let me describe the ordering guarantee we get, because people assume more than they should. Within one process, messages published in sequence are written to each socket in that same sequence, and TCP preserves order, so every member sees the same order. That's true as long as there is a single Node process, and it's a lovely property. The moment we have multiple servers, nothing guarantees it, and we'll need to think about it again with Redis Streams, where ordered ids come from.

One more point on fan-out cost, which is memory rather than CPU. When we call `socket.write(frame)` with the same Buffer on a thousand sockets, Node doesn't copy it a thousand times up front, but each socket may hold a reference in its write queue until the kernel accepts the bytes. That's another reason the backpressure check matters: a slow client keeps a reference to every frame we queued for it. With a megabyte cap per client, we know the worst case for ten thousand slow clients, and we can size the machine, or simply drop them, with that number in hand.

That completes the in-memory pub/sub core: registry, rooms, publish. Try this experiment. Write a quick script that opens a thousand WebSocket clients, using the `ws` package just as a test tool, joins them all to one room, and sends a hundred messages. Watch the server's memory and CPU. You'll learn where it bends. Next chapter, we face the problem we've been ignoring: clients that disappear without telling us, and keeping presence accurate.

Welcome to chapter five. Everything so far assumed that clients leave politely. They send a close frame or the TCP connection ends, we get an event, and we clean up. Real networks are less kind. A user closes a laptop, walks into an elevator, switches from wifi to cellular, or a NAT box silently drops an idle mapping. In none of these cases does our server see anything. This lecture is about why that happens and how to detect it.

Recall the half-open connection from the TCP lecture. Our server believes the socket is established. It will happily write to it, and those writes go into the kernel's send buffer. TCP will retransmit with exponential backoff, and only after many retries, typically a few minutes by default on Linux, does the kernel give up and report an error. In the meantime, Pulse shows that person as online, and publishes keep queuing bytes for a ghost. You may say, doesn't TCP have keepalive? It does. `socket.setKeepAlive(true, 30000)` in Node turns on TCP keepalive probes after thirty seconds of idleness. It helps, and I do recommend setting it, but it isn't enough. The defaults at the OS level are often two hours, the probe interval and count are system-wide settings, and many proxies and load balancers terminate TCP themselves, so a keepalive probe may be answered by the proxy and tell you nothing about the actual client behind it.

That's the key insight: liveness has to be checked at the application layer, end to end. If the client answers a message that travels through every hop, the whole path works. The WebSocket protocol was designed with exactly this in mind. It has control frames, ping and pong, that ride on the same connection. The server sends a ping, a compliant client must answer with a pong quickly, and the browser does this automatically without any JavaScript, which is delightful.

There's a second reason for application-level heartbeats: idle timeouts. Cloud load balancers close connections that carry no traffic. AWS's classic load balancer defaults to sixty seconds, nginx has `proxy_read_timeout` defaulting to sixty seconds as well. If your chat room is quiet for a minute, the proxy will kill a perfectly healthy connection. Regular pings generate traffic and keep the connection open. So the same mechanism gives us both dead-peer detection and keep-alive through intermediaries. Let's define the failure detector we'll build. Every thirty seconds, for each client, check a flag. If the flag says the client hasn't answered the previous ping, terminate the connection. Otherwise, set the flag to false and send a ping. When a pong arrives, set the flag back to true. That means a dead peer is detected within one to two intervals, so between thirty and sixty seconds. It's simple, it's the pattern used by the ws library, and it's tunable.

What should happen at termination? We call `socket.destroy()`, not a graceful close, because a graceful close would try to send a close frame to a peer that isn't listening and wait for a reply that never comes. destroy tears the socket down immediately, which fires our close handler, which runs `dropClient`, which removes the client from rooms and the registry. And in the next lectures, that same event will drive the presence broadcast. Let's write the ping and pong loop.

Open `src/heartbeat.js`. The RFC says a ping is a control frame with opcode 0x9, and a pong is opcode 0xA. Control frames may carry up to 125 bytes of payload, must not be fragmented, and a pong must echo the payload of the ping it answers. We already wrote encodeFrame with an opcode parameter, so sending a ping is `socket.write(encodeFrame(0x9, Buffer.alloc(0)))`. Let's write a `start(registry, dropClient)` function that sets up the interval. Here's the loop. `const timer = setInterval(() => { for (const client of registry.all()) { if (!client.isAlive) { dropClient(client.id, 'heartbeat-timeout'); continue } client.isAlive = false; client.socket.write(encodeFrame(0x9, Buffer.alloc(0))) } }, 30000)`. Read it slowly. On every tick, any client that still has isAlive false never answered the last ping, so we drop them. Everyone else gets marked false and receives a fresh ping. Their pong must flip the flag back before the next tick.

Now the receiving side. In `handleFrame` in server.js, the case for opcode 0xA, which we previously ignored, becomes `record.isAlive = true`. And while we're here, any frame at all from the client is also proof of life, so I like to set `isAlive = true` and `lastSeen = Date.now()` at the top of handleFrame, for every opcode. A client that is busy sending chat messages shouldn't be dropped just because its pong was delayed behind a large frame.

One thing to be careful about is mutating the registry inside the loop. `dropClient` removes entries from the Map while we iterate it. As I said before, deleting during Map iteration is defined behavior in JavaScript, but I prefer to collect dead ids in an array and drop them after the loop. Also call `timer.unref()` so the interval doesn't keep the Node process alive on shutdown, and export a `stop` function that clears it, which makes tests clean.

Let's test it with a real half-open connection, which is easy to fake. Connect a client with `nc` after a manual handshake, or simpler, use a small Node script that completes the handshake and then simply never reads or answers. Set the interval to three seconds for the test, using an environment variable like `HEARTBEAT_MS`. Within about six seconds you should see `heartbeat-timeout` in the logs and the client count drop. Configurable intervals are not optional, because nobody wants a thirty-second wait in a test suite.

Compare this with the browser. Browsers answer pings automatically at the protocol level, below JavaScript. That means the page can't observe pings, and it means a frozen tab with blocked JavaScript still answers, since the browser's network stack does it. That's actually good for us, and also a limitation. The server can only know the browser process is reachable, not that the page code is healthy, and if we ever need that, we add an application-level heartbeat message on top.

That brings up the reverse direction. The client also wants to know the server is alive, but the browser WebSocket API doesn't expose ping frames, so the client can't send them. The standard approach is an application message, for example the client sending `{ type: 'ping' }` every twenty-five seconds and the server replying `{ type: 'pong' }`, and the client reconnecting with backoff if no reply arrives within ten seconds. We'll put that in `public/index.html`, and the server side is a one-line case in the message handler.

Now we have accurate liveness, so we can build presence, the green dots. Presence means the set of users currently online in a room, kept up to date as people come and go. Create `src/presence.js`. The first question is where presence state lives. It's derived data: a user is present in a room if at least one live connection of theirs is a member of that room. So we don't store a separate list we have to keep in sync. We compute it from the registry and rooms.

The function is `listPresence(room)`. `const ids = rooms.members(room)`, then map each id through the registry to a record, drop the missing ones, and return `{ name, status, since }` objects. But remember the multi-tab case: one person with two tabs has two connections. We want one entry per user, so we group by name using a Map, and mark them as active if any of their connections is active. That grouping is the difference between a presence list that looks right and one with duplicates.

Status. Let's support two values: active and idle. A client is idle if `Date.now() - lastSeen` is more than, say, two minutes. We already update lastSeen on every frame. But here's a design question: should a pong count as activity for idle purposes? If so, nobody would ever be idle, since the browser pongs automatically. So we separate two fields. `lastPong` is for liveness and `lastActive` is updated only on real application messages like say, or a `{ type: 'activity' }` message the client sends on mouse or keyboard events, throttled to once every fifteen seconds.

Next, change notifications. Presence is only useful if it's pushed. We emit a presence event whenever membership or status changes, which means on join, on leave, on disconnect, and when a user crosses the idle threshold. The payload is the full list: `{ type: 'presence', room, users }`. Sending the full snapshot rather than a diff is a conscious trade-off. Snapshots are idempotent and self-healing, since a lost or reordered message gets corrected by the next one. Diffs are smaller but fragile. For rooms up to a few hundred users, snapshots are fine.

To avoid a storm, we debounce. If fifty people join a room within a second, say at a conference, sending fifty snapshots to fifty members is two thousand five hundred messages for nothing. So presence changes mark the room dirty, and a timer flushes dirty rooms every, say, five hundred milliseconds, sending one snapshot each. In code, `const dirty = new Set()`, `function markDirty(room) { dirty.add(room) }`, and a `setInterval` that publishes `listPresence(room)` for each dirty room and clears the set.

Hook it in. In `rooms.join` and `rooms.leave`, call `presence.markDirty(room)`. In `dropClient`, before leaving rooms, grab the list of rooms the client was in, and mark each dirty after removal. When a new client joins, we also send them an immediate snapshot privately, so they don't wait for the next flush. And when a heartbeat times out, the same path fires, so a ghost user disappears from everyone's sidebar within the heartbeat window, typically under a minute. Let's see the whole thing. Open three tabs as three users. Watch the sidebar fill. Close a tab: the dot disappears quickly via the close frame. Now disable wifi on one machine, or kill a tab's network with the devtools offline toggle, and within the heartbeat window that user disappears. That is presence with real failure detection, and it's the core of Pulse. Next chapter: everything we've done lives in one process's memory, and I'll show you exactly where that breaks.

Here's the uncomfortable truth about everything we've built. Our registry is a JavaScript Map. Our rooms are Sets. They live in the memory of one Node process. As long as Pulse is a single server, that's perfect. But a single process has limits, a single core, a single machine, and a single point of failure. Sooner or later you need two processes, and the moment you start a second one, the design breaks in a very specific way. Let's see it.

Start two copies of Pulse, one on port 4000 and one on 4001, using a `PORT` environment variable. Connect Asha's browser to 4000 and Ben's browser to 4001, and both join the general room. Asha sends a message. `rooms.publish('general', ...)` runs in process one, loops over its own Set, and finds only Asha. Ben is in process two's memory, which has no idea the message exists. Ben sees nothing. Presence is split in the same way: each side thinks the room has one user.

This isn't a bug we can patch with a little code. It's structural. In-memory pub/sub is, by definition, scoped to one address space. To fix it, the processes must communicate. Whenever a message is published on one, the other must hear about it and deliver it to its own local members. That means we need a shared medium, something both processes can publish to and subscribe from, and that's the role of a message broker. Let's think about what options exist for that medium. You could have the servers talk to each other directly, an all-to-all mesh, where each knows every peer's address. That works for three nodes and becomes painful at thirty: membership, discovery, and N squared connections. You could use a database, polling a table for new rows, which brings back all the polling problems from chapter one. Or you can use a purpose-built broker that handles fan-out of messages between publishers and subscribers. Redis is the most common choice, and it's already fast and simple.

Notice the architecture that results. Each Pulse process still owns its own sockets, its own registry, and its own local rooms. Those can't be shared, since a socket can't leave its process. What changes is that publish does two things: deliver to local members, and publish the message to the broker. And each process subscribes to the broker, and when it receives a message published by another process, it delivers it to its local members only. We're splitting delivery into a local part and a distributed part.

There's a subtle trap in this design: the echo. If process one publishes to Redis and also subscribes to Redis, it will receive its own message back and deliver it to its local members a second time. Everyone on process one would see every message twice. There are two fixes. Either you don't deliver locally, and rely on the broker for everything, or you tag each message with the originating server id and ignore your own. We'll use the first approach for simplicity, as one code path is easier to reason about.

Also think about what the broker costs us. It adds a network hop, so a message that used to be a function call is now a round trip to Redis, typically under a millisecond on the same network. It adds a dependency that can fail. And it forces us to ask which semantics we need: fire-and-forget delivery, or something durable that survives a subscriber being offline. Redis offers both, pub/sub and Streams, and the next two lectures take them in turn.

Redis pub/sub is the simplest possible broker. A publisher sends a message to a named channel with `PUBLISH channel message`, and returns the number of subscribers that received it. A subscriber sends `SUBSCRIBE channel`, and from then on, Redis pushes messages to it as they arrive. You can try it right now in two terminals with redis-cli. In one, run `SUBSCRIBE room:general`. In the other, `PUBLISH room:general hello`. The first terminal prints the message immediately. There are some important semantics to internalize. Pub/sub is fire and forget. Redis does not store the messages. If no subscriber is connected at the moment of the PUBLISH, the message is simply gone, and PUBLISH returns zero. There's no acknowledgement, no replay, and no history. Delivery is at-most-once. For live chat and presence signals, that's often exactly right, since stale presence is useless anyway, but we must know it going in.

Another rule: a connection that has issued SUBSCRIBE enters subscriber mode. In that mode it can only issue subscribe, unsubscribe, ping and a few similar commands. It can't run normal commands. So every Node process needs two Redis connections: one for subscribing and one for everything else, including publishing. With the `redis` package, that's `const pub = createClient(); const sub = pub.duplicate(); await pub.connect(); await sub.connect()`. Forgetting this gives you a confusing error the first time you PUBLISH on the subscriber connection.

Let's write `src/bus.js`. It exports `publish(channel, payload)` and `subscribe(channel, handler)`. publish does `pub.publish('pulse:' + channel, JSON.stringify(payload))`. I prefix every key and channel with `pulse:` to namespace our app inside a shared Redis. subscribe calls `sub.subscribe('pulse:' + channel, (raw) => handler(JSON.parse(raw)))`. Note that the redis client invokes the listener with the message string and the channel name, so we parse inside a try and catch, since another service could publish garbage on the same channel. Now connect the rooms module. When the first local client joins a room on this process, we call `bus.subscribe('room:' + name, deliverLocal)`, and when the last local member leaves, `sub.unsubscribe('pulse:room:' + name)`. This is important: a process only subscribes to rooms it actually has members in. With ten thousand rooms and ten processes, each process subscribes only to its relevant few hundred, so Redis doesn't push irrelevant traffic to everyone. That's the benefit of rooms as channels.

And `rooms.publish` changes. Instead of looping over local members, it calls `bus.publish('room:' + room, payload)` and returns. The subscription handler is what loops over local members and writes the frame. So the path for a chat message is: client frame arrives, handler validates, publish goes to Redis, Redis fans out to every subscribed Pulse process, each delivers to its local sockets. Every process, including the origin, uses the same delivery code. That avoids the double-delivery trap we described.

Let's rerun the experiment. Two Pulse processes on 4000 and 4001, Redis running locally, Asha on one and Ben on the other, both in general. Asha speaks, and Ben sees it. Our cross-process problem is solved. Be aware of the limits though. Redis pub/sub has no persistence, a subscriber that reconnects after a network blip misses everything in between, and a new user joining can't see history. For that we need something that remembers. That's Redis Streams, next.

Redis Streams are an append-only log. Think of it as a durable, ordered list of entries, where each entry has a unique id and a set of field-value pairs. You append with `XADD`, and the id is generated by Redis, in the form of a millisecond timestamp, a dash, and a sequence number. This is the missing piece for Pulse: message history, replay after reconnect, and reliable delivery. Try it in redis-cli: `XADD pulse:stream:general * from asha text hello`. The star means auto-generate the id.

Reading. `XRANGE pulse:stream:general - +` returns every entry from the earliest to the latest, and `XREVRANGE pulse:stream:general + - COUNT 50` returns the latest fifty, newest first. That's exactly what we need when a user joins a room: show the last fifty messages. And to follow new entries live, `XREAD BLOCK 5000 STREAMS pulse:stream:general $` blocks for up to five seconds waiting for anything newer than now. The dollar sign means only new entries from this moment. Because ids are ordered, Streams give us something pub/sub never did: a resume point. Suppose a client disconnects after seeing entry id 1728212345678-0. When it reconnects, it sends that id, as a `lastEventId`, and the server calls `XRANGE pulse:stream:general (1728212345678-0 +`, where the opening parenthesis makes the range exclusive, and sends what was missed. That's the same idea as the Last-Event-ID in server-sent events, and it makes flaky mobile connections tolerable.

Now the write path in Pulse. In `src/stream.js`, `async function append(room, msg) { const id = await client.xAdd('pulse:stream:' + room, '*', { from: msg.from, text: msg.text, ts: String(msg.ts) }, { TRIM: { strategy: 'MAXLEN', strategyModifier: '~', threshold: 1000 } }); return id }`. Streams grow forever unless trimmed, so we cap at roughly a thousand entries with MAXLEN tilde, which allows Redis to trim in efficient chunks. The returned id becomes the message's id for clients. So how do pub/sub and Streams combine? I'd recommend this: on a say, first XADD to the stream to get the canonical id and persist it, then PUBLISH the message, including its id, on the live channel for instant fan-out. Pub/sub is the fast path for connected clients and the stream is the source of truth for history and recovery. A client that reconnects uses the id of the last message it saw to ask for the gap. Two tools, each doing what it's good at.

There's another feature, consumer groups. With `XGROUP CREATE pulse:stream:events workers $ MKSTREAM` you create a group, and then several workers each run `XREADGROUP GROUP workers worker-1 COUNT 10 BLOCK 5000 STREAMS pulse:stream:events >`. Redis hands each entry to exactly one consumer in the group. A worker acknowledges with `XACK pulse:stream:events workers <id>`, and unacknowledged entries stay in a pending list, which you can inspect with `XPENDING` and reclaim with `XAUTOCLAIM`. That gives at-least-once processing. To make the stream path concrete in code, here is the history fetch used when someone joins. `async function recent(room, count) { const rows = await client.xRevRange('pulse:stream:' + room, '+', '-', { COUNT: count }); return rows.reverse().map((r) => ({ id: r.id, ...r.message })) }`. We reverse the results, because XREVRANGE returns newest first and the UI wants oldest first. The handler sends this as `{ type: 'history', room, messages }` right after the joined acknowledgement, and from then on the live pub/sub messages continue. The ids make it trivial to deduplicate any message that appears in both.

Where would Pulse use a consumer group? For background work off the hot path, like writing messages to a database, sending push notifications to offline users, or computing analytics. A group of workers shares the load, a crashed worker's pending entries are reclaimed by another, and the realtime path never waits on any of it. Rule of thumb: pub/sub for ephemeral fan-out to every listener, Streams when you need history, replay or work distribution. Now let's scale the servers themselves.

Last chapter. We now have several Pulse processes sharing messages through Redis. The next question is how clients get to those processes. Put yourself in front of a load balancer with three Pulse servers behind it. A browser connects, and the balancer picks a server. For a WebSocket, that single connection lives on that server for its whole life, so the balancing decision is made once. Where does stickiness matter, then? It matters in three places. First, the upgrade handshake can be split across requests in some setups. If you use a fallback transport, like socket.io's long-polling that later upgrades to WebSocket, the session spans several HTTP requests, and every one of them must hit the same server, otherwise the server answering has no record of the session. Second, a reconnect: when a client reconnects, it would ideally return to a server that still holds its session state. Third, any state you keep in process memory, like a rate limiter or a half-sent upload.

Pure WebSocket, as we built, is simpler. Once the connection is upgraded, it's pinned by TCP to one backend, because the load balancer proxies the bytes of that one connection. Different clients land on different backends, which is just what we want. So for Pulse, strict sticky sessions aren't required for correctness, since all shared state is in Redis. They're a nice optimization for reconnects, and they're mandatory if you add a long-polling fallback. How is stickiness implemented? The common methods are IP hash, where the balancer hashes the client's source address to pick a backend, and cookie-based affinity, where the balancer sets a cookie naming the backend, then routes by it. IP hash is simple but unfair when many users share an address behind a corporate NAT, so one backend gets a heap of them. Cookies are more even, but need cookie support, and API clients that aren't browsers may not keep them.

The real danger of relying on in-process state shows up when a server dies or you deploy. All the sockets on that process close at once, and thousands of clients reconnect simultaneously. This is the thundering herd. Without care, they hammer the remaining servers, each doing a handshake, joining rooms, and fetching history, and the overload can cascade into a second failure. The mitigation lives in the client: reconnect with exponential backoff and random jitter, for example waiting a random time up to one second, then two, then four, capped at thirty.

Let me write that client logic, because it belongs in `public/index.html`. `let attempt = 0; function connect() { const ws = new WebSocket(url); ws.onopen = () => { attempt = 0; resume() }; ws.onclose = () => { const delay = Math.random() * Math.min(30000, 1000 * Math.pow(2, attempt)); attempt++; setTimeout(connect, delay) } }`. Full jitter, meaning the whole delay is randomized, spreads the herd more evenly than adding a small jitter to a fixed delay. A quick word on health checks, since stickiness and balancing both depend on knowing which backends are alive. The balancer should probe each Pulse process with a plain HTTP GET to a `/healthz` endpoint, which we can answer from the same TCP server by recognizing a normal request that has no Upgrade header. It returns 200 while the process is accepting connections and 503 once it begins draining on SIGTERM. That way the balancer stops sending new connections to a server that's shutting down, before its existing sockets are closed, and deploys stay invisible to users.

And on reconnect, the client sends `{ type: 'resume', room, lastId }`, using the last message id it saw. The server answers with an XRANGE from the stream, filling the gap, regardless of which backend the client lands on. That's the beauty of putting history in Redis rather than in process memory: any server can resume any client. Stickiness becomes an optimization, not a requirement. Next, let's look at the Redis side of that arrangement properly.

Let's consolidate Redis's role. In a horizontally scaled Pulse, Redis is the shared brain. It's the message broker, through pub/sub channels per room. It's the durable log, through Streams for history and replay. And it can also hold presence state that must be visible across processes. Let me show how that last piece works, because our in-memory presence computation from chapter five only sees local sockets, and that's now wrong. Think about the problem. Asha is on server one and Ben on server two, both in general. If each server computes presence from its local registry, each snapshot has one name. We need a cluster-wide view. The classic pattern is a Redis set per room with expiry-based membership. Each server, for each local user, periodically writes `ZADD pulse:presence:general <now> asha`, a sorted set using the timestamp as score. To list who is online, run `ZRANGEBYSCORE pulse:presence:general <now minus 60000> +inf` to get everyone who's been refreshed in the last minute.

Why a sorted set with timestamps, and not a plain set with add and remove on connect and disconnect? Because of crashes. If a server process dies, it never runs its disconnect handlers, so its users would stay in a plain set forever. With timestamps, entries age out on their own. The server refreshes its users' scores on every heartbeat tick, and anything not refreshed within the window is considered gone. It's self-healing, and it's the same philosophy as the heartbeat itself: absence of proof of life means dead.

Keep it tidy with a periodic `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE pulse:presence:general -inf <now minus 120000>` to delete the expired entries, so the set doesn't grow. For a more fine-grained approach, you can use per-user keys with a TTL: `SET pulse:presence:general:asha 1 EX 45`, refreshed on each heartbeat. When the key expires, the user is gone. With keyspace notifications enabled, Redis can even publish an event on expiry. Both work, and I prefer the sorted set for listing a room in one command.

When presence changes, we still need to tell clients. Each server publishes a small event, `PUBLISH pulse:presence:general changed`, and every server subscribed to that channel, meaning every server with members in that room, reacts by reading the sorted set and pushing a fresh snapshot to its local members. The event carries no data and the snapshot is read from the source of truth, so ordering and duplication problems don't matter. That's our debounced snapshot design from last chapter, now with Redis as the truth.

Now let's talk about failure modes honestly. Redis is a single point of failure in this design. If it goes down, cross-server messages stop, though local WebSocket connections remain up. A well-behaved Pulse server should keep serving its local sockets, keep trying to reconnect to Redis, and report itself degraded. The `redis` client reconnects automatically with a strategy you can configure, and you should handle the `error` event on both clients, because an unhandled error event will crash the process, same as sockets.

For high availability in production, you'd run Redis with replicas and Sentinel, or use Redis Cluster, though pub/sub in cluster mode broadcasts to all nodes, and sharded pub/sub with `SSUBSCRIBE` and `SPUBLISH`, available since Redis 7, is the more scalable option. Those are operations topics, but know they exist. Also remember the throughput ceiling: a single Redis handles hundreds of thousands of small operations a second, so for most apps, the broker won't be your bottleneck. The sockets will. Let's put a load balancer in front.

Final technical lecture. We have three Pulse processes, Redis, and now we need a front door. I'll use nginx as the load balancer because it's common and simple to read, but the concepts apply to HAProxy, Envoy, or a cloud load balancer. WebSockets need special handling, since by default nginx speaks HTTP/1.0 to backends and strips the Upgrade headers, so the handshake fails. Create `nginx.conf` with an upstream block: `upstream pulse { server 127.0.0.1:4000; server 127.0.0.1:4001; server 127.0.0.1:4002; }`.

Then the server block. `location /ws { proxy_pass http://pulse; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade"; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_read_timeout 120s; }`. Each directive has a reason. HTTP version 1.1 is required for Upgrade. The two headers forward the upgrade intent, because Upgrade is a hop-by-hop header that proxies normally drop. And proxy_read_timeout governs how long nginx tolerates silence from the backend before closing, so it must be longer than our thirty-second heartbeat interval. Balancing algorithms. The default is round robin, which spreads new connections evenly. But connection count, not request rate, is what matters for WebSockets, since a connection might live for hours. So `least_conn;` inside the upstream is better, as it sends a new connection to whichever backend has the fewest active ones. If you want stickiness, `ip_hash;` pins by client address. nginx's open-source edition doesn't have cookie stickiness built in, and the paid edition adds it. Our Pulse needs neither, but least_conn is a sensible default.

A few operational points. Each proxied WebSocket costs two sockets on the load balancer, one from the client and one to the backend, so file descriptor limits matter: raise `worker_connections` and the OS `ulimit -n`. Ephemeral port exhaustion can bite between the balancer and a single backend, since one source address has about sixty-four thousand ports to the same destination, so a very large deployment needs multiple balancer addresses or backend ports. Also, TLS termination typically happens at the balancer, meaning clients use `wss://` and the backends speak plain `ws://` on the private network.

Deploys are the next big topic. When you restart a backend, its sockets die. For a graceful deploy, the server should handle SIGTERM by stopping accepting new connections, sending each client a close frame with code 1001, going away, and then exiting after a grace period. Clients receiving 1001 reconnect with jitter, landing on other backends, where they resume from the stream. Rolling the three servers one at a time means the cluster as a whole never goes down. That's the value of keeping state out of the processes.

Let me verify the full system with you. Start Redis. Start three Pulse processes on 4000, 4001 and 4002. Start nginx. Open four browser tabs pointing at the balancer, with four different users, all joining general. Check the logs to see that the connections spread over the backends. Send messages from each tab, and every tab shows them. Check the presence sidebar lists all four. Then kill one backend with Ctrl-C and watch its clients reconnect to survivors, resume from the stream and show no gaps.

Let's wrap up the course. You built a WebSocket server from TCP up: the upgrade handshake with SHA-1 and the GUID, the frame parser with masking and opcodes, a client registry, rooms with fan-out, ping and pong for failure detection, presence derived from heartbeats, then Redis pub/sub and Streams to cross process boundaries, and nginx in front. The main lessons are these. Always buffer bytes. Assume peers die silently. Keep payloads identical for fan-out. Put shared state in a shared store. And make clients reconnect with jitter. Where to go next? Try binary protocols, rate limiting, authentication, and load testing with thousands of connections. Thanks for building along with me.
